question: Q4 — What is the capitalisation threshold? The de minimis safe harbour allows expensing items under $2,500 with an election on the return. Without a stated firm threshold, every tool purchase is a judgement call — and on this client it was a judgement call made 127 times.
working: The authority printed here never states a capitalisation threshold. It states a CEILING on one and leaves the threshold itself to the taxpayer: 1.263(a)-1(f)(1)(i)(B)(1) and (f)(1)(ii)(B)(1) both condition the safe harbour on the taxpayer having, at the beginning of the taxable year, accounting procedures expensing 'property costing less than a specified dollar amount' - specified by the taxpayer, not by the regulation. The ceiling is $5,000 per invoice or item with an applicable financial statement ((f)(1)(i)(D)) and $2,500 without it (the $500 in (f)(1)(ii)(D) as raised by Notice 2015-82). The IRS page adds that a book policy ABOVE the ceiling may still be deducted if it clearly reflects income, so even the ceiling is not a hard line. Two things must therefore come back before a number can be stated: the firm has to choose the policy amount and put it in place at the START of the year (it cannot be set retroactively at close, and the election under (f)(5) is irrevocable and must cover every qualifying item in the year), and someone has to establish whether this client has an applicable financial statement, which fixes which ceiling applies. The 127 judgement calls cannot be resolved by this desk; they are waiting on a firm policy decision plus that one client fact.

question: Q6 — Is a brewery a meal? Entertainment has been 100% non-deductible since the 2017 Act, and alcohol at a taproom is not a business meal.
position: A brewery tab is a food-or-beverage expense, not entertainment by virtue of the venue; it runs through the 50% limit if the § 1.274-12(a)(1) conditions are met.
working: The close's premise is that drinks at a taproom fail because they are not a meal. (b)(1) removes exactly that argument: 'Food or beverages means all food and beverage items, regardless of whether characterized as meals, snacks, or other types of food and beverages.' Beer is a beverage item, so the charge is a food or beverage expense governed by § 1.274-12, and by (a)(2) it is allowable at 50% if the (a)(1) conditions hold — not lavish, the taxpayer or an employee present, provided to the taxpayer or a business associate. It becomes non-deductible entertainment only by the route in § 1.274-11(b)(1)(ii), which is triggered by an entertainment activity, not by the name over the door. What still has to be established before the line is taken at 50%, and these are client facts: who was present, that at least one of them was a business associate under (b)(3), the business purpose and the other § 1.274-5T(b) elements, and whether anything else was on the same bill (a tour, a tasting event, tickets) that would make the drinks food provided at or during an entertainment activity.

question: Q7 — Are groceries ever deductible? Supermarket spending is personal unless it is job-site provision for a crew — in which case it may be 100% deductible rather than 50%, a third answer again.
working: The rule is clear and does not turn on the merchant. § 1.274-12(b)(1) makes groceries 'food or beverages' like any restaurant charge, so if they were provided to the taxpayer or a business associate — and (b)(3) counts an employee as a business associate — the 50% limit in (a)(2) applies. What is not established is the client fact the answer turns on: who consumed this food, where, and why. Household food for the owner's family never reaches § 1.274-12 at all; food bought to feed a crew at a job site does. Two further points the close should hear. First, nothing printed in this desk's record supplies a 100% answer for job-site crew food. The only routes out of the 50% limit here are the (c)(2) exceptions — expense treated as compensation and reported as wages, recreational or social events primarily for non-highly-compensated employees such as picnics and holiday parties, food made available to the general public, and food sold to customers for full consideration — and (c)(2)(iii)(A) expressly excludes meals whose value is excluded from employees' income under section 119 as furnished for the convenience of the employer. Routine crew feeding is not a picnic. Second, whichever percentage applies, § 1.274-5(c)(2)(iii)(A) requires documentary evidence for any expenditure of $75 or more. Ask the client: what was bought, for whom, at which site, and whether any of it was reported as compensation.

question: Q7 — Are groceries ever deductible? Supermarket spending is personal unless it is job-site provision for a crew — in which case it may be 100% deductible rather than 50%, a third answer again.
working: The rule in this record is clear on both halves. § 1.262-1(b)(5) sets the default — 'Except as permitted under section 162 or 212, the costs of a taxpayer's meals not incurred in traveling away from home are nondeductible personal expenses' — and § 1.162-1(a) states the only door out of it, ordinary and necessary expenditures directly connected with or pertaining to the taxpayer's trade or business. Which side of that line a supermarket charge falls on is a fact about the client that the close has not established: whether the food was eaten by the taxpayer's own household (personal under 1.262-1(a), and the card it was bought on does not change that) or provided to a crew at a job site as a cost of getting the work done. Nothing in this desk's record decides that from the receipt alone. Note also that this desk cannot supply the 100%-versus-50% answer the close is reaching for: § 1.162-1(b)(2) points out of this record for items not deductible, to sections 261-276, and those limitations are not printed here. Ask the client what was bought, for whom, and at which site.

question: Q8 — Is this clothing deductible? Work clothing is deductible only if it is not suitable for everyday wear. Trade workwear generally qualifies; ordinary retail clothing does not, whatever card it was bought on.
working: Nothing printed in this desk's record decides clothing for this client. There is exactly one clothing paragraph, § 1.262-1(b)(8), and it is written about a category of person my client is not: 'a member of the armed services'. Its test — deductible only to the extent the equipment 'is especially required by his profession and does not merely take the place of articles required in civilian life', illustrated by the deductible sword and the non-deductible uniform, with the companion paragraph on reservists' uniforms — is the right shape of test, and it decides on what the item is and what the profession requires rather than on who sold it. But it is confined by its own terms to servicemembers and to nontaxable-allowance arithmetic that has no counterpart here, and I will not extend it to a civilian taxpayer by analogy. The general rule the close states — deductible only if not suitable for everyday wear — does not appear in this record in any form. What is left is only the divide itself: § 1.262-1(a) bars personal, living and family expenses, § 1.162-1(a) allows ordinary and necessary expenditures directly connected with the trade or business, and neither tells me which one a garment is. § 1.262-1(c) lists the personal items deductible anyway and clothing is not among them, but that list is about sections 163 through 217 and is not a work-clothing rule either. This desk needs authority on work clothing for a non-military taxpayer before it can answer. Separately, and even with that authority, the answer would need facts the close has not given: what garment was actually bought and what the client's trade requires — not the card and not the store.

question: Are card rewards income? The common treatment is a reduction of purchase price rather than income — rebates on spending are generally not taxable. A chart with a Credit Card Rewards income account invites the opposite answer and overstates taxable income.
working: Nothing binding in this desk's record reaches a reward paid by a card ISSUER to the cardholder. The only paragraph squarely on credit-card rewards is PLR 201027015 (tier tertiary), and 'PLR 201027015, precedential value' says in its own words that under section 6110(k)(3) it 'may not be used or cited as precedent' — so it cannot carry an answer, however persuasive its reasoning. The price-adjustment paragraphs that ARE citable are all seller-to-buyer: Rev. Rul. 2005-28 (Pittsburgh Milk / Rev. Rul. 76-96) treats a payment 'from a seller to a purchaser' reaching an agreed net selling price as a purchase-price adjustment, IRS Pub. 525 'Cash rebates' covers a rebate 'from a dealer or manufacturer of an item you buy', and IRS Pub. 334 'Trade discounts' covers discounts from the supplier of the articles. A card issuer is neither the seller nor the supplier of what was bought, so applying those paragraphs to card rewards is an extension, not a citation. Pulling the other way, 26 CFR 1.61-1(a) is primary and sweeps in 'all income from whatever source derived, unless excluded by law', and Announcement 2002-18 expressly says the issues around promotional benefits are unresolved and that its non-enforcement relief does not extend to benefits converted to cash. The record therefore leaves the firm a choice it has to make and document, not a rule the desk can apply. Two facts would also have to be settled before any position: whether the reward was taken in cash or in kind, and whether the spending that earned it was the business's.

question: Q12 — Do payments to individuals create a 1099-NEC obligation? Peer-to-peer payments to individuals for services can. Does the workflow track payee totals, and does anything surface the threshold before January?
working: Nothing printed in this desk's record touches information reporting. The three sources are 1.263(a)-1 (capital expenditures), 1.162-3 (materials and supplies) and the IRS tangible property page - all of them about whether an amount paid for TANGIBLE PROPERTY is expensed or capitalised. None of them mentions Form 1099-NEC, payments for services, payee totals, a reporting threshold, or a January deadline. There is no paragraph here that could be stretched to reach it without inventing authority. This question belongs to a desk holding the information-reporting rules (section 6041/6041A and their regulations, and the Form 1099-NEC instructions), which this desk does not have.

question: Do payments to individuals create a 1099-NEC obligation? Peer-to-peer payments to individuals for services can. Does the workflow track payee totals, and does anything surface the threshold before January?
position: Yes — $2,000 or more paid in a year to a non-employee individual for services in the course of the business requires a Form 1099-NEC, filed and furnished by January 31, unless the payment ran over a payment card or third-party payment network.
working: That paragraph states the operative test directly: file Form 1099-NEC 'for each person in the course of your business during the year to whom you have paid at least $2,000 in ... Services performed by someone who is not your employee (including parts and materials)'. It is the paragraph carrying the threshold now in force — 'Instr. 1099-MISC/NEC (Rev. 12-2026), "Increase in threshold"' raised it to $2,000 for tax years beginning after 2025, which supersedes the $600 figure still printed in 26 CFR 1.6041-1(a)(1)(i); 26 USC 6041A(a) is the primary rule underneath it, requiring a return from a service-recipient in a trade or business at the dollar amount in effect under 6041(a). Two limits belong with the answer. First, the obligation attaches only to payments made in the course of a trade or business — 26 CFR 1.6041-1(b)(1) says section 6041(a) 'applies only to payments in the course of trade or business'; a purely personal payment to an individual creates nothing. Second, the payment rail can displace the obligation entirely: 26 CFR 1.6041-1(a)(1)(iv) and its Example 1 and Example 2 put payment-card and third-party-network transactions under section 6050W rather than 6041, and the settlement entity files the 1099-K instead — so a peer-to-peer payment made through a third-party payment network as defined in 26 CFR 1.6050W-1(c)(3) is not the payor's to report. What this desk cannot establish, and what has to go back to the firm: which payees crossed $2,000 in the calendar year, which are individuals rather than corporations, and which app or rail each payment ran over. Whether the software tracks payee totals or surfaces the threshold before January is not a question this desk's authority reaches at all — but 'Instr. 1099-MISC/NEC (Rev. 12-2026), "Filing dates"' and 26 USC 6071(c) fix the deadline at January 31, so any surfacing that first happens in January is already late for gathering W-9s.

question: Q16 — Where is the line between a tool and a fixed asset? The capitalisation threshold again, asked from the asset side. A single tool purchase in the hundreds is expensed under the safe harbour and capitalised without it, and Section 179 or bonus depreciation may apply either way.
working: Asked from the asset side, the same gap appears as in Q4: this authority draws no single line between a tool and a fixed asset. What it does draw is a floor and a ceiling with a taxpayer choice in between. The floor is definitional and needs no election - 1.162-3(c)(1)(iv) makes a unit of property costing $200 or less a material or supply, and (c)(1)(iii) does the same for one with an economic useful life of 12 months or less. Above that, whether a tool is expensed turns on the de minimis election, which is optional ('a taxpayer electing to apply'), whose dollar amount is the taxpayer's own 'specified dollar amount' under (f)(1)(i)(B)(1)/(f)(1)(ii)(B)(1), and whose ceiling depends on the AFS fact. And the IRS page's own answer forecloses reading the ceiling as the line at all: amounts above it are not forced into capitalisation, they simply fall back to 'the normal rules that apply'. Those normal rules for ACQUIRED property live in 1.263(a)-2, which is not printed in this desk's record, so this desk cannot state the line above the ceiling either. Two decisions must come back before this is answerable: the firm's own policy amount, in place at the beginning of the year, and whether the election is being made for the year at all. Section 179 and bonus depreciation, raised in the question, are outside every source printed here.

question: Q16 — Where is the line between a tool and a fixed asset? The capitalisation threshold again, asked from the asset side. A single tool purchase in the hundreds is expensed under the safe harbour and capitalised without it, and Section 179 or bonus depreciation may apply either way.
working: This desk holds one source, 1.263(a)-3, and that section is about amounts paid to IMPROVE tangible property already owned. Its own overview says so, and (d) requires capitalisation only of amounts paid to improve a unit of property, tested by whether activities performed AFTER the property is placed in service are a betterment, a restoration, or an adaptation to a new or different use. A tool bought at the hardware counter is an acquisition, not an improvement to an existing unit of property. The rules that would decide it - 1.263(a)-2 for costs to acquire or produce a unit of property, and 1.263(a)-1(f) for the de minimis safe harbour - are referred to by cross-reference inside this section but are not printed in this desk's record, and a cross-reference is not authority I may cite. The small-taxpayer safe harbour in (h) does not help either: it is limited to eligible BUILDING property. Noted deliberately: the capitalization-and-de-minimis desk was asked this same question and escalated for a different reason (the rule reaches it there, but leaves the threshold to the firm). Here the rule does not reach it at all.

question: Q18 — Does a hardware-store purchase ever become an asset? A year of small trade-supplier purchases will contain some that are not consumables. Only line detail separates them, and a bank feed has none.
working: The rule is clear; the facts are not. Every test printed here is applied item by item to a described thing: 1.263(a)-1(f)(1)(i)(D) and (f)(1)(ii)(D) measure the limit 'per invoice (or per item as substantiated by the invoice)'; (f)(3)(i) requires delivery, installation and similar costs on the SAME invoice to be added to the item's cost and, where one invoice covers several properties, allocated across them by a reasonable method before each is tested; and 1.162-3(c)(1) classifies by what the thing is and how long it lasts - a component to repair a unit of property, fuel or a similar item consumed within 12 months, a unit of property with a useful life of 12 months or less, or one costing $200 or less. A bank feed carries a merchant name and a total, which satisfies none of those tests. (f)(6), the anti-abuse rule, cuts the other way too: a single item cannot be split across componentised invoice lines to get under the limit, so the line detail is needed to see what the unit of property actually is. So: yes, a hardware-store purchase can be an asset, and which of the year's purchases are cannot be settled from the feed. Someone has to get the itemised receipts from the client for the trade-supplier purchases and, for anything installed into existing property, establish whether it was a repair or an improvement - the improvement rules in 1.263(a)-3 are not printed in this desk's record.

question: Q18 — Does a hardware-store purchase ever become an asset? A year of small trade-supplier purchases will contain some that are not consumables. Only line detail separates them, and a bank feed has none.
position: Yes, some of them are assets, and the bank feed can never tell you which - the purchase invoices must be obtained, and any asset among them carries its own permanent record.
working: This paragraph settles both halves of what the close actually raised. First, it treats assets as an ordinary category of what a business buys - 'Assets are the property, such as machinery and furniture you own and use in your business' - and requires records verifying when and how the asset was acquired, its purchase price, cost of improvements, section 179 and depreciation taken, how it was used, and how it was disposed of; the documents it names as showing that are purchase and sales invoices, closing statements and cancelled checks. So a purchase from a trade supplier does become an asset when it is such property, and it then needs a permanent record that an expense line does not. Second, on the bank feed specifically, the same paragraph is explicit that an account statement is admitted only as proof of PAYMENT, and that 'proof of payment of an amount, by itself, does not establish you are entitled to a tax deduction. You should also keep other documents, such as credit card sales slips and invoices, to show that you also incurred the cost.' The feed is that statement and nothing more, so it cannot support either the deduction or the asset record. What this desk does NOT decide is the tax classification test - which items over which amount must be capitalised - which is not in this record; it decides only that the invoice, not the feed, is the document that has to be in hand.

question: Q18 — Does a hardware-store purchase ever become an asset? A year of small trade-supplier purchases will contain some that are not consumables. Only line detail separates them, and a bank feed has none.
working: This desk's authority is about WHOSE expense it is, not about when an expense becomes an asset. 1.262-1 denies deductions for personal, living and family expenses; 1.162-1 describes what an ordinary and necessary business expense includes; Pub. 587 is entirely about business use of a home. None of it states a capitalisation rule, a threshold, a useful-life test, or a definition of a fixed asset. The closest text is 1.162-1(a), which lists 'supplies, incidental repairs' among business expenses and parenthetically points at section 263 for commissions - a cross-reference, not a rule I may cite, and section 263 is not printed here. Reaching for it would be exactly the stretch this desk is meant to refuse. If the intended question for THIS desk is instead whether the hardware-store purchases are business at all rather than household spending, that is answerable from 1.262-1(a) in principle, but only once the itemised receipts exist - which is the same missing line detail the question already names. As asked, though, the gap is authority, not facts.

question: Are rewards revenue at all? See Q9, "Are card rewards income?"
working: Same defect as Q9, and it bites harder here because the question is where rewards belong on the face of the books. To say rewards are not revenue, the desk would have to rest on 'PLR 201027015, Ruling request (1)', which is the one paragraph in the record that actually addresses rewards on a credit card and concludes they are an adjustment to purchase price rather than an accession to wealth — but 'PLR 201027015, precedential value' says the ruling 'is directed only to the taxpayers requesting it' and 'may not be used or cited as precedent'. A tertiary source that disclaims its own precedential value cannot support a book-treatment position. The alternative footing is no better: IRS Pub. 334 'Trade discounts' tells you not to show a discount 'separately as an item in gross income', but it is about the difference between stated and actual prices paid to the supplier of the articles, and a card issuer's reward is not that; Rev. Rul. 2005-28's holding is confined to Medicaid Rebates incurred by a pharmaceutical manufacturer, and its 'EFFECT ON OTHER DOCUMENTS' paragraph shows the Service itself has left part of the rebate question open and says taxpayers may not rely on the suspended conclusion. Against that, 26 CFR 1.61-1(a) is the only primary paragraph reaching the question and it starts from inclusion. So the record does not settle whether a rewards credit is revenue, a reduction of the expense it arose from, or neither — the firm has to pick a treatment and apply it consistently, and that choice should be recorded rather than inferred from a chart of accounts. It also cannot be answered in the abstract: whether the reward arose on business or personal spending, and whether it was redeemed for cash, is a fact about the client.

question: Personal spending on a business card is not "excluded" — it is a draw. The money left the business account either way. Booking it nowhere makes the bank unreconcilable by exactly the amount of it.
position: The disbursement has to be entered in the books — an item the books are missing is corrected by making the entry, not by leaving it out; this desk cannot say which account receives the offset.
citation: IRS Pub. 583 (12/2024), "Reconciling the checking account" — what the books are updated for
working: That paragraph is the firm's own recorded position and it is directly on the point the close raised. Reconciling exists to 'Make sure that your checkbook and books reflect all bank charges and the correct balance in the checking account', and the procedure ends: 'Update your checkbook and journals for items shown on the reconciliation as not recorded (such as service charges) or recorded incorrectly. At this point, the adjusted bank statement balance should equal your adjusted checkbook balance.' A card charge that cleared the account and was booked nowhere is exactly an item 'shown on the reconciliation as not recorded'. It is not the other kind of difference: the companion paragraph, 'what the statement did not yet include', covers deposits made after the statement date and checks that had not cleared — timing items that are reconciling items with no entry in the books. Personal spending on the business card is not a timing item, so 'exclude it' leaves the books permanently out by that amount, which 26 CFR 1.446-1(a)(4) also forbids in its own terms: a taxpayer 'must maintain such accounting records as will enable him to file a correct return', including 'a reconciliation of any differences'. What this desk cannot establish, and does not: which account takes the other side. Nothing in 26 CFR 1.446-1 or Pub. 583 in this record names an owner's draw, a distribution, or a due-from-shareholder, and Pub. 583's 'Bookkeeping System' paragraph only describes debits and credits generically. Whether the cost is the business's at all is the personal-or-business desk's question, and the equity-versus-receivable classification behind the word 'draw' is settled by neither desk's authority as printed here — that half needs the firm.

question: Personal spending on a business card is not "excluded" — it is a draw. The money left the business account either way. Booking it nowhere makes the bank unreconcilable by exactly the amount of it.
working: This desk can settle only half of what was asked, and it is not the half the question turns on. On its own half the record is clear: 26 CFR 1.262-1(a) allows 'no deduction ... for personal, living, and family expenses' except as expressly provided, and 26 CFR 1.162-1(a) confines business expenses to 'ordinary and necessary expenditures directly connected with or pertaining to the taxpayer's trade or business'. Which card was swiped changes neither test, so personal spending charged to a business card is not the business's expense and is not deductible — subject to 26 CFR 1.262-1(c), which lets certain personal items (interest, taxes, medical, charitable and so on) through under their own sections, so what was actually bought still has to be established. But the question asked is what the item IS in the books — that it is a draw rather than an exclusion. Nothing in this desk's record reaches that. Sections 1.262-1 and 1.162-1 govern deductibility; IRS Pub. 587 governs business use of a home. None of them names a draw, a distribution, an owner's equity account, or any offsetting entry, and none of them says what happens to cash that left a business account for a non-deductible purpose. Rather than reason from 'not deductible' to 'therefore a draw' — which would also depend on the entity type, since a draw, a distribution and a shareholder receivable are different things and the entity is not established here — the desk escalates that half. The cash-and-bank desk establishes that the disbursement must be entered in the books; naming the account is a call for the firm.

question: Q33 — Is streaming television ever a business subscription? Entertainment streaming on a business card is personal unless there is a waiting room.
position: An entertainment streaming subscription is an entertainment expenditure disallowed by § 1.274-11(a); a waiting room does not convert it, though the client's own trade could.
working: Watching entertainment television is an activity of a type generally considered to constitute entertainment, amusement or recreation, and by § 1.274-11(b)(2) an 'expenditure' includes amounts paid for goods, services and facilities, so a subscription is within the disallowance in (a). The objective test in (b)(1)(iii) is what settles the close's specific argument: an activity generally considered entertainment 'will be treated as entertainment ... regardless of whether the expenditure can also be described otherwise', and the test expressly 'precludes arguments that entertainment means only entertainment of others or that an expenditure for entertainment should be characterized as an expenditure for advertising or public relations'. A screen in a waiting room is entertainment of others offered as goodwill, which is precisely the recharacterization the paragraph forecloses. The same paragraph leaves one real opening, and it is a client fact rather than a legal one: 'in applying this test the taxpayer's trade or business is considered', which is why the professional theatre critic attending in a professional capacity is not entertained. If the client's trade is reviewing, licensing, producing or otherwise professionally consuming this content, the answer changes and I would need that fact. One limit on this position the firm should know: § 1.274-11(c) preserves the section 274(e)(1)-(9) exceptions, and the text of those exceptions is printed in this desk's record only in its food-and-beverage form under § 1.274-12(c)(2). I therefore cannot resolve here whether a public-availability exception could reach a screen shown to whoever walks in; I can only say the general rule disallows it and the goodwill argument does not survive the objective test.

question: Q33 — Is streaming television ever a business subscription? Entertainment streaming on a business card is personal unless there is a waiting room.
working: This desk's record holds no paragraph about subscriptions, services bought for a premises, or entertainment. It holds the general divide only: § 1.262-1(a) bars personal, living and family expenses, and § 1.162-1(a) allows the ordinary and necessary expenditures 'directly connected with or pertaining to the taxpayer's trade or business'. That rule is clear, and what it turns on is a fact about the client that the close has not established — who watches this subscription, on what screen, and for what. A service running in a client-facing waiting area is a different fact pattern from a household account that happened to be paid on the business card, and the card it was paid on does not decide it, any more than incidental business use of a residence makes rent deductible under § 1.262-1(b)(3). The Pub. 587 material printed here is about identifiable space in a home used exclusively and regularly for business; it does not reach a subscription, and I will not run a streaming service through an exclusive-use test written for rooms. Ask the client where the subscription is used and by whom. One caveat even if the business connection comes back established: § 1.162-1(b)(2) sends the reader to sections 261-276 for items not deductible, and those provisions are not in this desk's record — a separate limitation may disallow the cost regardless of the answer to the personal-or-business question.
